newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No problems seen with next Russian IMF tranche.
newsitem.headline: No problems seen with next Russian IMF tranche.

text.p: Russia appears to be broadly fulfilling the terms of its $10 billion loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund and the IMF is likely to pay out the next instalment of the credit, economists said on Tuesday.

An IMF official said a Fund mission that was in Moscow last week to review Russia's economic performance had left and the Fund's board of directors would decide whether to pay the August tranche in the first half of September.
A Finance Ministry economist said the IMF appeared satisfied with Russia's performance.

"We have reached an understanding on all questions," Pavel Zhukov, head of the ministry's macroeconomic department, told Reuters. "The mission does not have claims which have an insurmountable character and it looks as though it is satisfied with how we carry out our obligations."

Under the terms of the three-year credit agreed in March -- the second-largest granted by the IMF -- the Fund sends a team of experts to Moscow every month to see whether Russia is making progress on cutting inflation and reviving its economy.
It then makes a recommendation to the IMF board on whether to pay out another monthly tranche of around $330 million.
The Fund delayed payment of the July tranche because of worries that the low level of tax collection in the first half of this year was bloating the budget deficit.
But it gave the green light to the payment two weeks ago after the Russian authorities took steps to boost revenues by countering tax evasion and scrapping exemptions.
If Russia's finances were on the right track then, they will also have seemed in order to the team which has just left and which will make a recommendation on the August instalment.
"The basic picture can't have changed that much between the two points," said an economist close to the talks.
The next IMF mission is due in Moscow in mid-September.
The latest one conducted a monthly review, checking Russia's performance on a series of financial indicators such as money supply and the budget deficit.
It also conducted a quarterly review under a programme looking at structural reforms including privatisation, natural monopolies, the social safety net and banking reform.

The economist said things were not perfect here either, as Russian officials were distracted by the campaign for the presidential election. But he said Fund experts believe the authorities are trying to get things moving again.

"There have been delays compared with the initial plan that was finalised in March," he said. "But as long as there's a critical mass of positive progress, I don't think the board would delay any programme for any time."

The brightest spot in structural reform is banking, where the central bank has recently tightened supervision of Russia's more than 2,000 banks amid renewed worries that there could be a widespread banking crash.
"Banking would seem to be one sector where there's been more progress than others," the economist added.
